corpus_explorer <- df %>% select( track_name, artist_name_s, genres, popularity, duration_ms, danceability, energy, loudness, speechiness, acousticness, liveness, valence, tempo, instrumentalness ) %>% mutate(duration = round(duration_ms / 60000, 2)) %>% select(-duration_ms) %>% rename( track name = track_name, artist name(s) = artist_name_s )```

title: Background & Corpus
text:
Research Question
Do my favorite songs share underlying patterns in Spotify audio features despite differences in genre, language, and artist?
This project explores whether personal music preferences can be explained through measurable audio characteristics, using a playlist of my 100+ favorite tracks.

title: Background & Corpus
text:
The Playlist




The corpus is based on a personal Spotify playlist consisting of over 100 tracks.
Rather than being curated by genre or artist, the playlist reflects individual listening preferences — songs that stand out as favorites over time.

title: Background & Corpus
text:
The Corpus
The dataset spans Dutch, English, and Spanish repertoire across rap, trap, R&B, pop, and soul.
Despite this apparent diversity in genre, language, and artist, the key question is whether these tracks share common underlying characteristics.
This analysis focuses on identifying patterns that may explain why these songs are consistently preferred.

title: Background & Corpus
text:
Top Artists & Genres
The playlist contains a wide range of artists and genres, but some occur more frequently than others.
The top 5 most frequent artists are: - The Weeknd (12 tracks)
- Tory Lanez (6 tracks)
- Frenna (4 tracks)
- Sevn Alias (4 tracks)
- Brent Faiyaz (3 tracks)
In terms of genre, the top 3 occurring genres are: - Rap
- R&B
- Drill
At the same time, the playlist remains diverse, with many other artists and genres appearing less frequently.
The dataset includes songs in three main languages: - English
- Dutch
- Spanish

title: Background & Corpus
text:
Approach
This project applies computational analysis to uncover patterns within the playlist.
Key steps include: - Extracting Spotify audio features (e.g. energy, danceability, tempo, valence)
- Analyzing distributions of these features across all tracks
- Identifying recurring patterns and potential clusters
- Comparing perceived diversity with measurable similarity
The goal is to determine whether subjective music preferences align with objective, data-driven characteristics.

title: Background & Corpus
text:
Assumptions

Spotify audio features approximate perceptual musical qualities

Personal listening preferences reflect underlying patterns that can be quantified

Feature-based analysis provides deeper insight than genre labels alone

title: Chroma Features

Interpretation
The chromagram shows recurring activation of specific pitch classes over time, indicating a stable tonal centre and repeated harmonic patterns.

title: Chroma Features
text:
What this means
Rather than exhibiting harmonic complexity or frequent modulation, the track relies on loop-based harmonic structures. These repeating pitch distributions align with a consistent and recognisable musical foundation.

title: Chroma Features
text:
Connection to the research question
Although the playlist appears stylistically diverse, this suggests that harmonic behaviour may be more consistent than expected across tracks.

title: Chroma Features
text:
Key Insight
The playlist shows harmonic consistency through stable tonal centres and repetition.

title: Loudness & Energy
text: Correlation Matrix

title: Loudness & Energy
text:
Interpretation
Energy and loudness are strongly positively correlated (r = 0.75), while energy is negatively correlated with acousticness (r = -0.67).

title: Loudness & Energy
text:
What this means
Tracks in the playlist are structured around production intensity. High-energy tracks tend to be louder and less acoustic, reflecting modern production styles.

title: Loudness & Energy
text:
Connection to the research question
This suggests that the playlist is not only rhythmically consistent, but also consistent in its production characteristics.

title: Loudness & Energy
text:
Key Insight
The playlist favours high-energy, compressed production over acoustic variation.

Interpretation
The self-similarity matrix shows strong temporal continuity with subtle structural segmentation.

title: Timbre Features
text:
What this means
Changes in timbre are gradual rather than abrupt. Structural transitions are driven more by layering and density than by strong timbral contrast.

title: Timbre Features
text:
Connection to the research question
This suggests that timbre is not the primary driver of variation within the playlist.

title: Timbre Features
text:
Key Insight
Structure is shaped more by harmonic repetition than timbral contrast.
